h:
For decades, one of the largest collections of Ethiopian Christian manuscripts in the world remained on microfilm.

More than 9,000 manuscripts were photographed across Ethiopia between 1973 and 1994, many from churches and monasteries that had preserved them for centuries.

The material survived, but access remained limited.

Researchers often had to rely on physical microfilm, printed catalogues, incomplete descriptions, and specialist archives unfamiliar to most readers.

That is now changing.

The Hill Museum & Manuscript Library has completed the digitization of its Ethiopian Manuscript Microfilm Library collection. Thousands of manuscripts can now be viewed through its online Reading Room, while detailed cataloguing continues. The first 5,000 records have been completed online, with more still being processed.

The collection is not limited to biblical manuscripts.

It includes Gospel books, Psalters, homilies, liturgical texts, saints’ lives, church records, legal documents, historical chronicles, illuminated pages, and other works preserved within the Ethiopian Christian tradition.

Taken together, they preserve a large part of Ethiopia’s Christian literary memory.

Western Christian history is often told through Greek manuscripts, Latin fathers, Roman councils, European libraries, and Reformation disputes.

Those sources matter, but they do not represent the whole Christian record.

Ethiopia preserved one of the oldest continuous Christian traditions in the world, along with a broader biblical canon, a substantial Ge’ez literary culture, and an ecclesial memory that developed outside the usual Western frame.

The issue was never that Ethiopia had nothing to examine.

The issue was that much of the material remained difficult to access.

Digitization does not settle every claim made about the Ethiopian tradition. A scanned manuscript still has to be dated, translated, compared, and placed within its historical setting.

But the evidence is now easier to inspect.

Researchers can compare biblical manuscripts, study canon tables, trace scribal traditions, examine marginal notes and illustrations, and identify texts that may have received limited attention outside Ethiopian studies.

That matters for the study of Enoch, Jubilees, Meqabyan, the history of the Ge’ez Bible, and broader questions about what Ethiopia preserved, when it preserved it, and how those books were used.

This is not a story about 9,000 secret books being discovered.

They were already known.

The important development is that one of Christianity’s least accessible manuscript collections is becoming easier to study.

The manuscripts were not lost.

The archive is simply becoming more visible.
